[2] The claimant set out his allegations in the narrative portion of his Personal Information Form, (PIF).2 In sum, he states that as a Roma person he has experienced discrimination in all facets of public life. The discrimination began at school, where his classroom was segregated between Roma and non-Roma students. It has followed him since. Quite literally, the claimant describes being followed in stores. Following on the substandard education he alleged he received, he has been unable to find good, paying work on a consistent basis. The claimant has also found himself to be the victim of random attacks by non-Roma Hungarians. The police took no action when he complained to them.
ISSUES

[3] The issues that are determinative of this hearing are identity, credibility, and state protection.
Identity

[4] The claimant's personal identity and his identity as a Hungarian citizen were established to the panel's satisfaction through the identity documents presented at the hearing, namely, a copy of his Hungarian passport3 as well as his oral testimony, which fixed him in and identified him as a citizen of that country.
The Claimant's Roma Identity

[5] To establish his Roma identity, the claimant submitted a document from the Roma
Ethnicity Self Government in the town of XXXX.4 Issued at the claimant's request, the certificate confirmed the claimant's ethnicity, stating that he was born in the town of XXXX, Hungary. Taking the totality of the evidence and testimony into consideration the panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant has established that he is Roma.
Credibility

[6] At the heart of the claim for protection is the question of whether the claimant is able to meet his onus to credibly establish that he has a well-founded fear of persecution in Hungary. The claimant states that two events give rise to his fear. The first occurred in XXXX 2010 when five men jumped him as he was going home on his bicycle. The men got out of a car, beat him, and knocked out his front teeth. He managed to reach his home where his mother dressed his wounds. He testified that a sympathetic dentist attended to his dental needs. When the claimant and his mother tried to file a police report, they were turned away. The police told them that they could not file a report because they did not know the names of the men who attacked him.

[7] The incident left the claimant scared to go to the city. He went only when it was necessary. However, in XXXX 2011, he had cause to go to the pharmacy. Once again he was attacked. This time he was stopped by several men he was trying to pass. They spit on him and beat him. However, they stopped their attack when a passerby shouted at them. Considering it useless to make a complaint, the claimant did not go to the police. Instead he decided that he would leave Hungary and come to Canada, which he did with the financial assistance of friends.

[8] Several questions arose from the claimant's account of how and why he came to Canada. First, while the claimant testified that it was his friends in Hungary who helped him with the cost of his ticket, his ticket was purchased and issued from a travel agent in XXXX XXXX, Ontario. The panel found that this was not in keeping with what could be expected in the circumstances. The panel put the question to the claimant, who did not offer a rational explanation for why his ticket was bought in Canada as opposed to Hungary. He disclaimed all knowledge of the circumstances surrounding the purchase, stating "The only thing I know is that they helped me from home, to come from home and the only thing I did was to go to that airplane."

[9] The panel concluded that the claimant was not being straightforward, because by this time his former common-law partner was already in Canada. By the time he arrived on XXXX XXXX, 2011, she had been living here for some three months. He admitted that she was the reason he came to Toronto. He was coming to be with her. In light of this personal history, the panel infers that it is more likely than not that it was the claimant's common-law spouse who purchased his ticket. The panel finds that this lack of straightforwardness surrounding what is after all an easily explained event did not inspire confidence in the claimant's credibility.

The Incident of August 2010

[11] The panel asked the claimant about his front teeth as he had stated they had been kicked out during the incident of XXXX 2010. In response to the panel, the claimant testified that his front teeth had been kicked out during a fight that he became involved in. He showed the panel the gap where his front teeth were missing. When asked, he responded that he has been without front teeth for "approximately a year and a half maybe two years." As this response appeared to be inconsistent with the narrative, the panel gave the claimant the opportunity to explain. He then stated that he could not remember exactly when he lost his front teeth and proceeded to give a completely different rendering of the alleged incident. In the version related at the hearing, the claimant and his family were on their way home when they saw a fight. Although, they tried to avoid it, somehow, they became involved in it. The claimant told his spouse to leave quickly however, he was stuck in the fight and was hurt.

[12] The panel drew the claimant's attention to the fact that his oral testimony about the incident was fundamentally different from the version in his narrative. In his narrative, the claimant was by himself, he was riding his bicycle home when a car stopped beside him and his attackers, members of the Hungarian Guard, came out of the car and beat him.5 Asked which version of the story was the correct version, the claimant, initially, was silent, when he did respond he stated that he did not know, he could not remember exactly. After ascertaining that it was the claimant who had told the story to the person who helped him write the narrative and that it had been translated back to him, the claimant commented that he did not really understand the process at the time he made the claim, and that he had never been in front of a judge and found the process strange. He later stated that he understood only about a half of what was translated back to him.

[13] Counsel for the claimant also asked him about the incident and the inconsistency between his narrative and his oral testimony. Despite her best efforts, she was unable to elicit a coherent explanation from the claimant for the difference in the two versions. In response to her questions, he said he could not remember the incident clearly. He had no explanation for why he could not remember it. Asked by counsel whether he recalled being with his family at the time he was attacked he said he did. He also told her that he could remember being with them because "everybody remembers their family; you cannot forget them." However, he still could not explain why there was no mention of his family in the narrative.

[14] Upon considering all the circumstances surrounding both the alleged events and the making of the claimant's PIF, the panel concluded that he had not provided a satisfactory explanation for this major inconsistency. The panel's reasons are, that the claimant came to Canada in early XXXX 2011. The attack allegedly occurred in XXXX 2010. He filed his PIF in January 2012, which was less than two years after the incident. In the panel's view, the claimant could reasonably be expected to render a more accurate version of the events when he filed his PIF back in January 2012. Thus, absent a satisfactory explanation, the description of completely different circumstances surrounding the incident, namely, the addition of the presence of family members and coming upon a fight as opposed to being set upon by five men who alit from a vehicle is a circumstance that goes directly to the claimant's credibility.

[15] The panel is not persuaded that the inconsistency can be explained by a lack of sophistication on the part of the claimant, or because he did not completely understand what was translated back to him. If, as the claimant testified, this was the incident that convinced him to leave Hungary, the events would have been very traumatic, and likely oft-recounted by the claimant. Certainly they would have been fresher in his memory in 2012. Furthermore, the claimant had ample opportunity prior to the hearing to correct the narrative even with recently retained counsel, but did not do so. Accordingly, the panel finds that the unexplained inconsistencies provide valid reason to doubt and to reject the claimant's allegation of being set upon and attacked and having his front teeth kicked out. The panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, that members of the Guard did not attack and beat the claimant in August 2010.

[16] Furthermore, with respect to the claimant's front teeth, the panel found that he equivocated when asked about their loss. As stated earlier, he first responded that he lost his teeth about a year and a half maybe two years ago, leaving an open question as to when exactly he lost his teeth. As the claimant claims he did not seek medical attention at the time and as the panel has found that his credibility about the incident is compromised, the panel cannot be certain that the claimant lost his teeth at the time and in the manner he claimed.
The Incident of XXXX 2011

[17] The claimant alleged a second beating in XXXX 2011. When the panel asked him about this incident he responded that he could not remember it. Asked by his counsel how many times he had been attacked while he was in Hungary, the claimant responded "several times." Counsel for the claimant submitted that his difficulty during the hearing likely stemmed from injuries he might have received during these attacks. She also submitted that he had cognitive difficulties and had been put into a special school. The panel rejects these submissions because there was no evidence put before the panel to suggest that the claimant's injuries had resulted in cognitive difficulties. Secondly, while the claimant stated in the supplement to his PIF that he had been placed in a "special" school for mentally challenged people, he did not suggest that he was himself mentally challenged. Rather, the charge was that because he was placed in such a school he was not taught how to read and to write and was illiterate, although he did admit that he could read a little but found comprehension difficult.

[18] The documentary evidence is replete with statements attesting to the practice of putting Roma children into "special" schools for the mentally challenged. An example of which can be found at Item 13.5 of the Board's National Documentary Package (NDP) for Hungary.6 The Response to Information Request (RIR) addressed the situation of Roma, including employment, housing, education, healthcare, political participation etc. With respect to the placement of Roma children in special schools or classes for children with disabilities, the RIR states the following:
Sources indicate that Roma children are disproportionally placed in special schools or classes for children with disabilities or special needs (ibid. 9 June 2015, 30; UN 27 May 2016). According to ECRI, this "constitutes another form of segregated education because activities in these facilities are separated and different from those associated with regular education" (Council of Europe 9 June 2015, 30). The same source cites the Roma Education Fund as reporting that the percentage of Roma students in special schools ranges from 20 percent to 90 percent (ibid.). Sources indicate that "culturally biased" testing contributes to the misplacement of Roma children in special schools (ERRC [2016]; CFCF et al. Sept. 2015, 9).
In 2013, the European Court of Human Rights ruled on a case (Horvath and Kiss v. Hungary) involving two Roma students who were placed in a special school for children with mental disabilities and found that their rights were breeched under Article 2 of Protocol 1 (right to education) and Article 14 (prohibition against discrimination) of the ECHR (Council of Europe 9 June 2015, 30-31). The judgement of the Court indicated that Hungary has "a long history of wrongful placement of Roma children in special schools" and expressed concern about "the more basic curriculum followed in these schools and, in particular, the segregation which the system causes" (ibid., 31).The ERRC states that, despite this ruling and other judicial rulings deeming school segregation in Hungary as unlawful, "no action has been taken by the authorities to promote inclusive education. On the contrary, the evidence makes it clear that the government intends to pursue policies that further entrench racial discrimination into Hungary's school system" (ERRC 26 May 2016).

[19] The clear inference to be drawn from these statements is that the placement of Roma children into schools or classes for the mentally challenged is in no way reflective of the intellectual capacity of an individual Roma child. Therefore, with nothing more than the bare assertion that the claimant was placed in a special school for the mentally challenged, the panel is not prepared to find, as Counsel submitted, that he has intellectual challenges such that his capacity to provide reliable testimony is undermined.

[20] Therefore, taking all of the above into consideration, the panel finds that it is not persuaded that these events occurred. The panel accepts that as a Roma man, the claimant may have been subjected to discrimination and harassment, however, there is no persuasive evidence before it that could allow the panel to find that the claimant had ever, personally, been attacked in the manner he claimed. Based on the foregoing, the panel finds that the claimant has not met his onus to establish by means of credible and trustworthy evidence that he has a well-founded fear of persecution in Hungary.
STATE PROTECTION/ COUNTRY CONDITIONS

Nonetheless, upon considering the totality of the evidence including the country documentation as well as counsel's submissions, the panel finds, relying on Kotai7 that the claimant retains the onus of showing that state protection would not be available to him in Hungary.

subthemes.text:
[21] The claimant provided oral testimony that was inconsistent with his written narrative regarding his attempts to obtain state protection. When the panel asked him whether he had filed a police report about the August 2010 incident, he said he had not. However, his reason why he did not differed from his written narrative significantly. In the narrative he and his mother were prevented from filing a report because he did not know the names of his attackers. However, the claimant testified that he did not make a police report because he was afraid of a second attack and because he was afraid for his family. He stated that his attackers were masked, leaving their eyes as the only part of their face that he could see and what he saw caused him to fear his attackers. When he was attacked in XXXX 2011, he did not attempt to file a report.

[22] Having found that the claimant has not met his onus to establish by means of credible and trustworthy evidence that these incidents did in fact occur, the panel is not persuaded that the claimant has ever sought and been refused state protection.

[23] The panel acknowledges that the country documentation indicates that there is widespread intolerance and discrimination against the Roma, as a group, in Hungary. Many outlets report and comment on the same incidents. Nonetheless, upon considering the totality of the evidence including the country documentation as well as counsel's submissions, the panel finds, relying on Kotai7 that the claimant retains the onus of showing that state protection would not be available to him in Hungary. In Kotai, the Federal Court opined that,
The country conditions [in Hungary] do not suggest that the situation is so bleak that all Roma, regardless of their particular circumstances, should not be expected to make reasonable efforts to seek state protection before seeking refugee protection in another country.
The burden is on the claimant to provide clear and convincing evidence that the state is either unwilling or unable to provide him with adequate protection. The panel is not obliged to provide proof that the state can offer its citizens effective protection, rather the claimant bears the legal burden of rebutting the presumption that state protection exists by adducing clear and convincing evidence which satisfies the panel, on a balance of probabilities.

After ascertaining that it was the claimant who had told the story to the person who helped him write the narrative and that it had been translated back to him, the claimant commented that he did not really understand the process at the time he made the claim, and that he had never been in front of a judge and found the process strange. He later stated that he understood only about a half of what was translated back to him.

[13] Counsel for the claimant also asked him about the incident and the inconsistency between his narrative and his oral testimony. Despite her best efforts, she was unable to elicit a coherent explanation from the claimant for the difference in the two versions. In response to her questions, he said he could not remember the incident clearly. He had no explanation for why he could not remember it. Asked by counsel whether he recalled being with his family at the time he was attacked he said he did. He also told her that he could remember being with them because "everybody remembers their family; you cannot forget them." However, he still could not explain why there was no mention of his family in the narrative.

[14] Upon considering all the circumstances surrounding both the alleged events and the making of the claimant's PIF, the panel concluded that he had not provided a satisfactory explanation for this major inconsistency. The panel's reasons are, that the claimant came to Canada in early XXXX 2011. The attack allegedly occurred in XXXX 2010. He filed his PIF in January 2012, which was less than two years after the incident. In the panel's view, the claimant could reasonably be expected to render a more accurate version of the events when he filed his PIF back in January 2012. Thus, absent a satisfactory explanation, the description of completely different circumstances surrounding the incident, namely, the addition of the presence of family members and coming upon a fight as opposed to being set upon by five men who alit from a vehicle is a circumstance that goes directly to the claimant's credibility.

[15] The panel is not persuaded that the inconsistency can be explained by a lack of sophistication on the part of the claimant, or because he did not completely understand what was translated back to him. If, as the claimant testified, this was the incident that convinced him to leave Hungary, the events would have been very traumatic, and likely oft-recounted by the claimant. Certainly they would have been fresher in his memory in 2012. Furthermore, the claimant had ample opportunity prior to the hearing to correct the narrative even with recently retained counsel, but did not do so. Accordingly, the panel finds that the unexplained inconsistencies provide valid reason to doubt and to reject the claimant's allegation of being set upon and attacked and having his front teeth kicked out. The panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, that members of the Guard did not attack and beat the claimant in August 2010.

[16] Furthermore, with respect to the claimant's front teeth, the panel found that he equivocated when asked about their loss. As stated earlier, he first responded that he lost his teeth about a year and a half maybe two years ago, leaving an open question as to when exactly he lost his teeth. As the claimant claims he did not seek medical attention at the time and as the panel has found that his credibility about the incident is compromised, the panel cannot be certain that the claimant lost his teeth at the time and in the manner he claimed.
The Incident of XXXX 2011

[17] The claimant alleged a second beating in XXXX 2011. When the panel asked him about this incident he responded that he could not remember it. Asked by his counsel how many times he had been attacked while he was in Hungary, the claimant responded "several times." Counsel for the claimant submitted that his difficulty during the hearing likely stemmed from injuries he might have received during these attacks. She also submitted that he had cognitive difficulties and had been put into a special school. The panel rejects these submissions because there was no evidence put before the panel to suggest that the claimant's injuries had resulted in cognitive difficulties. Secondly, while the claimant stated in the supplement to his PIF that he had been placed in a "special" school for mentally challenged people, he did not suggest that he was himself mentally challenged. Rather, the charge was that because he was placed in such a school he was not taught how to read and to write and was illiterate, although he did admit that he could read a little but found comprehension difficult.

[18] The documentary evidence is replete with statements attesting to the practice of putting Roma children into "special" schools for the mentally challenged. An example of which can be found at Item 13.5 of the Board's National Documentary Package (NDP) for Hungary.6 The Response to Information Request (RIR) addressed the situation of Roma, including employment, housing, education, healthcare, political participation etc. With respect to the placement of Roma children in special schools or classes for children with disabilities, the RIR states the following:
Sources indicate that Roma children are disproportionally placed in special schools or classes for children with disabilities or special needs (ibid. 9 June 2015, 30; UN 27 May 2016). According to ECRI, this "constitutes another form of segregated education because activities in these facilities are separated and different from those associated with regular education" (Council of Europe 9 June 2015, 30). The same source cites the Roma Education Fund as reporting that the percentage of Roma students in special schools ranges from 20 percent to 90 percent (ibid.). Sources indicate that "culturally biased" testing contributes to the misplacement of Roma children in special schools (ERRC [2016]; CFCF et al. Sept. 2015, 9).
In 2013, the European Court of Human Rights ruled on a case (Horvath and Kiss v. Hungary) involving two Roma students who were placed in a special school for children with mental disabilities and found that their rights were breeched under Article 2 of Protocol 1 (right to education) and Article 14 (prohibition against discrimination) of the ECHR (Council of Europe 9 June 2015, 30-31). The judgement of the Court indicated that Hungary has "a long history of wrongful placement of Roma children in special schools" and expressed concern about "the more basic curriculum followed in these schools and, in particular, the segregation which the system causes" (ibid., 31).The ERRC states that, despite this ruling and other judicial rulings deeming school segregation in Hungary as unlawful, "no action has been taken by the authorities to promote inclusive education. On the contrary, the evidence makes it clear that the government intends to pursue policies that further entrench racial discrimination into Hungary's school system" (ERRC 26 May 2016).

[19] The clear inference to be drawn from these statements is that the placement of Roma children into schools or classes for the mentally challenged is in no way reflective of the intellectual capacity of an individual Roma child. Therefore, with nothing more than the bare assertion that the claimant was placed in a special school for the mentally challenged, the panel is not prepared to find, as Counsel submitted, that he has intellectual challenges such that his capacity to provide reliable testimony is undermined.

[20] Therefore, taking all of the above into consideration, the panel finds that it is not persuaded that these events occurred. The panel accepts that as a Roma man, the claimant may have been subjected to discrimination and harassment, however, there is no persuasive evidence before it that could allow the panel to find that the claimant had ever, personally, been attacked in the manner he claimed. Based on the foregoing, the panel finds that the claimant has not met his onus to establish by means of credible and trustworthy evidence that he has a well-founded fear of persecution in Hungary.
STATE PROTECTION/ COUNTRY CONDITIONS

[21] The claimant provided oral testimony that was inconsistent with his written narrative regarding his attempts to obtain state protection. When the panel asked him whether he had filed a police report about the August 2010 incident, he said he had not. However, his reason why he did not differed from his written narrative significantly. In the narrative he and his mother were prevented from filing a report because he did not know the names of his attackers. However, the claimant testified that he did not make a police report because he was afraid of a second attack and because he was afraid for his family. He stated that his attackers were masked, leaving their eyes as the only part of their face that he could see and what he saw caused him to fear his attackers. When he was attacked in XXXX 2011, he did not attempt to file a report.

[22] Having found that the claimant has not met his onus to establish by means of credible and trustworthy evidence that these incidents did in fact occur, the panel is not persuaded that the claimant has ever sought and been refused state protection.

[23] The panel acknowledges that the country documentation indicates that there is widespread intolerance and discrimination against the Roma, as a group, in Hungary. Many outlets report and comment on the same incidents. In Kotai, the Federal Court opined that,
The country conditions [in Hungary] do not suggest that the situation is so bleak that all Roma, regardless of their particular circumstances, should not be expected to make reasonable efforts to seek state protection before seeking refugee protection in another country.
The burden is on the claimant to provide clear and convincing evidence that the state is either unwilling or unable to provide him with adequate protection. The panel is not obliged to provide proof that the state can offer its citizens effective protection, rather the claimant bears the legal burden of rebutting the presumption that state protection exists by adducing clear and convincing evidence which satisfies the panel, on a balance of probabilities.

REASONS FOR DECISION

[1] The claimant, XXXX XXXX seeks protection in Canada pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).1 He alleges a well-founded fear of persecution in his native Hungary by reason of his ethnicity. The claimant is Roma.
ALLEGATIONS

[2] The claimant set out his allegations in the narrative portion of his Personal Information Form, (PIF).2 In sum, he states that as a Roma person he has experienced discrimination in all facets of public life. The discrimination began at school, where his classroom was segregated between Roma and non-Roma students. It has followed him since. Quite literally, the claimant describes being followed in stores. Following on the substandard education he alleged he received, he has been unable to find good, paying work on a consistent basis. The claimant has also found himself to be the victim of random attacks by non-Roma Hungarians. The police took no action when he complained to them.

[3] The issues that are determinative of this hearing are identity, credibility, and state protection.
Identity

[4] The claimant's personal identity and his identity as a Hungarian citizen were established to the panel's satisfaction through the identity documents presented at the hearing, namely, a copy of his Hungarian passport3 as well as his oral testimony, which fixed him in and identified him as a citizen of that country.
The Claimant's Roma Identity

[5] To establish his Roma identity, the claimant submitted a document from the Roma
Ethnicity Self Government in the town of XXXX.4 Issued at the claimant's request, the certificate confirmed the claimant's ethnicity, stating that he was born in the town of XXXX, Hungary. Taking the totality of the evidence and testimony into consideration the panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant has established that he is Roma.

[6] At the heart of the claim for protection is the question of whether the claimant is able to meet his onus to credibly establish that he has a well-founded fear of persecution in Hungary. The claimant states that two events give rise to his fear. The first occurred in XXXX 2010 when five men jumped him as he was going home on his bicycle. The men got out of a car, beat him, and knocked out his front teeth. He managed to reach his home where his mother dressed his wounds. He testified that a sympathetic dentist attended to his dental needs. When the claimant and his mother tried to file a police report, they were turned away. The police told them that they could not file a report because they did not know the names of the men who attacked him.

[7] The incident left the claimant scared to go to the city. He went only when it was necessary. However, in XXXX 2011, he had cause to go to the pharmacy. Once again he was attacked. This time he was stopped by several men he was trying to pass. They spit on him and beat him. However, they stopped their attack when a passerby shouted at them. Considering it useless to make a complaint, the claimant did not go to the police. Instead he decided that he would leave Hungary and come to Canada, which he did with the financial assistance of friends.

[8] Several questions arose from the claimant's account of how and why he came to Canada. First, while the claimant testified that it was his friends in Hungary who helped him with the cost of his ticket, his ticket was purchased and issued from a travel agent in XXXX XXXX, Ontario. The panel found that this was not in keeping with what could be expected in the circumstances. The panel put the question to the claimant, who did not offer a rational explanation for why his ticket was bought in Canada as opposed to Hungary. He disclaimed all knowledge of the circumstances surrounding the purchase, stating "The only thing I know is that they helped me from home, to come from home and the only thing I did was to go to that airplane."

[9] The panel concluded that the claimant was not being straightforward, because by this time his former common-law partner was already in Canada. By the time he arrived on XXXX XXXX, 2011, she had been living here for some three months. He admitted that she was the reason he came to Toronto. He was coming to be with her. In light of this personal history, the panel infers that it is more likely than not that it was the claimant's common-law spouse who purchased his ticket. The panel finds that this lack of straightforwardness surrounding what is after all an easily explained event did not inspire confidence in the claimant's credibility.

[10] Furthermore, the claimant's testimony was inconsistent with his written narrative where he claims to have been separated from his former common-law spouse since 2009. All of which further undermines his credibility.

Also, at issue was the likelihood that he would face persecution if returned to Hungary and whether adequate state protection would be available to him. For the reasons set out above the panel finds that the claimant has not met his onus to establish by means of clear and convincing evidence either the basis of his claim or that adequate state protection would not be available to him in Hungary.

[26] Accordingly, the panel finds that XXXX XXXX is not a Convention refugee, neither is he a person in need of protection as defined in sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act.
